xanadu.name: Xanadu (the engine)
xanadu.desc:
Xanadu is a single-file browser application that turns any relation graph into a navigable 3D world. Rather than a flat node-and-line diagram, it treats the most-connected nodes as **suns** and the things they connect to as **planets** orbiting them, so structure becomes a galaxy of solar systems you fly through.

Tap a body to focus it and the view flattens into a 2D constellation of cards — the focused node ringed by its neighbours — where you read, edit and grow the graph. Editing happens in one place, the hold-to-edit box; the + button creates a node and opens that editor, where you name it and connect it. Graphs load from the launcher — server-side documents from the manifest, or your own JSON/zip files — and everything autosaves to the browser.

This graph *is* the app's own code: every node below is a JavaScript function from `index.html`, wired by the real call graph, with its source in the `code` field and an explanation here — so you can explore Xanadu by exploring Xanadu.

boot.name: boot (top-level script)
boot.desc:
The top-level body of the `<script>` — the code that runs the moment the page loads, outside any named function. It creates the renderer, wires every DOM event handler (pointer gestures on the `#stage` surface, buttons, sliders, file inputs) to its interaction function, starts the animation loop, and then decides what to show: the saved graph if there is one, otherwise the launcher.

Most of this node's edges are that wiring — each hooks a control (the Load button, the + and ⊸ buttons, the zoom slider, the Connectors and Groups buttons, and so on) to the function that handles it.

index_html.name: index.html
index_html.desc: `index.html` is the entire engine. Its `<head>` carries the CSS, its `<body>` holds the static DOM the app mounts into — the WebGL canvas, the fixed controls, the panels and the overlay containers — and a single `<script>` holds every function in this graph. It has no build step and no dependency beyond JSZip (loaded to read and write zipped graph bundles); the graph documents live alongside it in `graphs/`.

graphs_manifest.name: graphs/manifest.json
graphs_manifest.desc:
`graphs/manifest.json` is the catalogue the launcher reads. It is a simple list, one entry per selectable document, each giving a title, a one-line description and the JSON filename in `graphs/`. The launcher renders a card per entry from this list.

It is the seam between the app and its content: adding a new graph to the picker means adding an entry here, with no code change. The manifest knows *which* documents exist; it does not contain the documents themselves.

graph_docs.name: graphs/*.json
graph_docs.desc:
The files in `graphs/` are the graph **documents** the engine renders — currently Greek Myth, the History of Jazz, Tudor & Elizabethan England, and this codebase graph. Each is a JSON object of `nodes`, `links`, `groups` and connector `types`.

This is exactly the shape the app produces when you export, and the shape `normalize` folds into the working model on load. Everything the engine does downstream — topology, layout, rendering, cards — operates on a document in this format, which is what lets the same engine present wildly different subjects.

dom_shell.name: HTML shell (body)
dom_shell.desc:
The HTML shell is the static `<body>` of `index.html` — the scaffolding the script mounts into. At its base sits the full-screen transparent input surface (`#stage`); a separate WebGL canvas above it draws the galaxy; layered above it are `<div>`s for the 2D cards (`#cards`), the collapsible HUD panel (`#hud`), the top bar (`#topbar`), the info cards and the overlay containers.

The division of labour is deliberate: the shell provides the fixed surfaces and mount points, while most of the *interactive* DOM — focus cards, the inline editor, the code lightbox, the launcher — is built at runtime by JavaScript. So the shell is small and stable; the busy, changing UI is generated on demand.

dom_controls.name: Floating controls & HUD
dom_controls.desc:
These are the floating controls and HUD: the zoom slider (`#zoomctl`), the spin-speed control and dial (`#spinctl`, `#spinpad`), the focus/galaxy toggle (`#togglefocus`), promote-to-sun, add-node and add-connection buttons, the connector and highlight toggles, the breadcrumb, and the collapsible control panel (`#hud`) and top bar (`#topbar`).

They are always present in the markup but not always visible: `floatControls()` shows or hides them according to the current mode, and the CSS state rules hide them entirely while the launcher or the inline editor is open. So the control surface adapts to what you're doing without each button managing its own visibility.

dom_editor.name: Structured editor DOM
dom_editor.desc: The editing DOM. The main editor is the hold-to-edit box — the `#planetinfo` card turned in place into a form for a node or connection: name, description, a Code Block, media and links, group, and, for nodes, a Connections section. Separately, the **Connectors** panel (`#typespanel`) and **Groups** panel (`#groupspanel`) edit the graph's connector types and groups, and the connection builder (`#connbuilder`) links any two nodes. The old standalone `#editor` panel has been removed — there is now one inline editor plus these focused panels.

dom_overlays.name: Info cards & overlays
dom_overlays.desc: The info cards and overlays that sit above the galaxy: the planet/relationship card and inline editor (`#planetinfo`), the relations panel (`#relinfo`), the image and video lightboxes (`#lightbox`, `#vidlb`), the embedded web view (`#webview`), the highlights list (`#hllist`) and the launcher (`#launcher`). They are plain `<div>`s toggled in and out as you tap into images, videos, links, connections and graphs.

css_tokens.name: CSS design tokens
css_tokens.desc:
These are the design tokens — the CSS custom properties that fix the app's dark palette and type scale in one place: the `--page` and `--card` backgrounds, the `--line` and `--line-strong` border colours, three tiers of text colour (`--t1`/`--t2`/`--t3`, brightest to dimmest), and a single `--accent`.

Everything else in the stylesheet is expressed in terms of these variables, so the whole look can be re-tuned by editing a handful of values. Note that *group* colours are resolved separately, by the JavaScript palette — these tokens govern the chrome, not the node colours. The node's `code` block holds the real `:root` definition.

css_state.name: CSS state / mode rules
css_state.desc:
These are the state, or "mode", rules — the trick that lets the app change how it looks by toggling a single class on `<body>`. Adding `launcher-active` or `card-editing` hides the floating controls with `display:none !important`, so the launcher and the inline editor can take over the screen without any JavaScript reaching in to hide each control individually.

It is a deliberately declarative pattern: `openLauncher` and `enterCardEdit` add the class, the CSS does the rest, and removing the class restores everything. The node's `code` block holds the actual rules. This is why the control-hiding is robust — it's one class flip, not a scatter of style writes.
css_state.code:
body.launcher-active #hud, body.launcher-active #cards, body.launcher-active #topbar, body.launcher-active #zoomctl, body.launcher-active #spinctl, body.launcher-active #spinpad, body.launcher-active #togglefocus, body.launcher-active #promotesun, body.launcher-active #addtempnode, body.launcher-active #addtempconn, body.launcher-active #toggleconn, body.launcher-active #highlightbtn, body.launcher-active #breadcrumb, body.launcher-active #bypassls, body.launcher-active #buildtag, body.launcher-active #hllist, body.launcher-active #planetinfo, body.launcher-active #relinfo{ display:none !important; }

body.card-editing #zoomctl, body.card-editing #spinctl, body.card-editing #spinpad, body.card-editing #togglefocus, body.card-editing #promotesun, body.card-editing #addtempnode, body.card-editing #addtempconn, body.card-editing #toggleconn, body.card-editing #highlightbtn, body.card-editing #breadcrumb, body.card-editing #bypassls, body.card-editing #buildtag, body.card-editing #hllist{ display:none !important; }

css_components.name: CSS component styles
css_components.desc:
These are the component styles — roughly 60 classes covering every built piece of UI: the 2D cards (`.card`), the launcher (`.lc-panel`, `.lc-card`), the connection builder (`.cb-panel`), the code preview (`.codeview`), the planet-card body (`.pf-desc`, `.pf-details`), the HUD bars and buttons, and the breadcrumb trail.

The JavaScript builders emit markup carrying these class names but no inline styling; all of the appearance lives here in the stylesheet. That separation is what lets a function like `makeCard` stay focused on structure while the CSS owns how it looks.

normalize.name: normalize()
normalize.desc:
`normalize(d)` is the gateway every graph document passes through before the app can render it. It takes a raw JSON document — which may be missing fields, use author-friendly shorthands, or have just arrived from an import — and folds it into a complete, self-consistent working model: it applies schema defaults, coerces the nodes and links into canonical form, and resolves each node's group to a concrete palette colour.

Crucially, it also builds the fast lookup structures the rest of the engine relies on: the ordered slug list, the slug-to-index map, and the adjacency and degree tables. From this point on, any node can be addressed by a stable integer index rather than by string id — which is what makes the layout, picking and rendering efficient. It runs via `load` whenever a document enters the model, so the raw document and the indexed model never drift apart.

load.name: load()
load.desc:
`load(d)` is `Model.load`, the single entry point for putting a document into the working model. It hands the raw document to `normalize` to apply defaults and build the index structures, then stores the returned result as the live model that the renderer, the layout simulation and the cards all read from.

It is called at three moments: on first boot with the fallback or saved document, whenever you open a different graph, and after any edit that changes the set of nodes or links. Routing all of those through one function is what keeps the indexed model in lockstep with whatever is currently on screen.

color_name.name: colorName()
color_name.desc:
`colorName(id)` resolves a single node to the *name* of its palette colour. It reads the node's group, looks up that group's assigned colour, and returns the colour name — falling back to a neutral gray when the node has no group, or its group has no colour set.

It is the shared source of truth for node colour. The star and planet renderer tints each body by it, and the legend lists groups by it, so the 3D galaxy and the legend can never disagree about what colour means what.

seeded_unit.name: seededUnit()
seeded_unit.desc:
`seededUnit(str)` is a small deterministic pseudo-random generator: given a string seed it returns a stable value in the range [0,1). Because the value is derived from the seed rather than `Math.random`, it is repeatable.

That repeatability is the whole point — it lets the initial layout be reproducible, so reloading a document lands its nodes in the same places rather than a fresh scatter each time. It is the deterministic randomness `seedInto` draws on.

seed_into.name: seedInto()
seed_into.desc:
`seedInto()` places the initial node positions before the force simulation begins. Rather than starting from pure noise, it spreads the nodes from a reproducible arrangement, giving the solver a sensible and deterministic starting point.

That determinism matters: the force simulation only *refines* an existing arrangement, and seeding it the same way each time means a given document settles into the same layout on every load instead of shuffling to something new. It draws its starting coordinates from `seededUnit`.

run.name: run()
run.desc:
`run(onDone, onProgress)` drives the force-directed layout to a settled arrangement. It runs a Barnes-Hut n-body simulation in which nodes repel one another and links pull them together, streaming progress through `onProgress` so the loading overlay can show the graph settle, and calling `onDone` once the layout has cooled.

Barnes-Hut is what makes this affordable at scale: distant clusters are approximated as single masses instead of computing every pairwise force, so large graphs still settle quickly. This is the streaming path; when the incremental route isn't available, `runSync` performs the same settling in one blocking pass.

run_sync.name: runSync()
run_sync.desc:
`runSync(n, E, onDone)` is the synchronous fallback for the force simulation, used when the streaming path isn't available. It settles the same n-body system in a single blocking pass and calls `onDone` when finished.

It trades the incremental progress of the streaming `run` for simplicity: no worker, no chunking, just run to completion. The result is the same settled layout — it's the reliable backstop that guarantees a graph always lays out, even where the preferred path can't run.

deg_factor.name: degFactor()
deg_factor.desc:
`degFactor(i)` scales a node's mass and repulsion in the force simulation according to its degree, so a highly connected hub pushes harder and claims more room than a leaf node.

Without this weighting, busy hubs would be crushed together with their many neighbours; with it, hubs carve out space and the settled layout takes on the readable hub-and-spoke structure that the whole solar-system metaphor depends on.

sh.name: sh()
sh.desc: `sh(type, src)` compiles a single GLSL shader of the given type from source, logs the compile error and returns null on failure. It is the lowest-level GPU building block, used by `link2` to assemble programs.
sh.code:
function sh(type,src){ const o=gl.createShader(type); gl.shaderSource(o,src); gl.compileShader(o);
    if(!gl.getShaderParameter(o,gl.COMPILE_STATUS)){ try{console.warn("PlanetGL shader:",gl.getShaderInfoLog(o));}catch(_){} return null; } return o; }

tex.name: tex()
tex.desc: `tex(w, h)` creates an empty RGBA WebGL texture of the given size with linear filtering — the raw render target the framebuffers draw into. A small helper used wherever `sizeFB` needs a fresh target texture.

fbo.name: fbo()
fbo.desc: `fbo(t)` creates a WebGL framebuffer with texture `t` attached as its colour target and returns it, so the renderer can draw into `t` off-screen. Paired with `tex` by `sizeFB` to build the offscreen targets for the bloom passes.
fbo.code: function fbo(t){ const f=gl.createFramebuffer(); gl.bindFramebuffer(gl.FRAMEBUFFER,f); gl.framebufferTexture2D(gl.FRAMEBUFFER,gl.COLOR_ATTACHMENT0,gl.TEXTURE_2D,t,0); return f; }

size_fb.name: sizeFB()
size_fb.desc: `sizeFB(dw, dh)` reallocates PlanetGL's offscreen framebuffers and their textures to match the current viewport — the full-resolution scene target plus the half-resolution targets used for the blur and bloom passes. It only reallocates when the size actually changes, freeing the old GPU resources first, so resizing never leaks textures.

draw_planets.name: drawPlanets()
draw_planets.desc: `drawPlanets(dw, dh, lightView, invView, count, dp)` issues the actual instanced draw for the planet spheres. It binds the planet shader and geometry, sets the per-frame uniforms — viewport, light direction, inverse-view matrix and time — and draws all `count` bodies in a single instanced pass. It is the innermost step of `render`, the one call that puts the lit planets on screen.

planetgl_init.name: init() — PlanetGL
planetgl_init.desc:
`init()` on the **PlanetGL** module is the WebGL2 setup — the heart of the 3D renderer. It creates the `#glcanvas` WebGL2 context, compiles and links the planet and label shader programs (through `sh` and `initLabels`), allocates the instanced-sphere geometry and the offscreen framebuffers used for the glow/bloom passes, and prepares the uniforms the draw path feeds each frame.

It runs once, invoked by the 2D `Renderer.init` which owns the visible canvas; PlanetGL then draws the lit planet spheres into its own layer that the renderer composites over the 2D backdrop. If WebGL2 is unavailable it bails early and the app falls back to the flat sprite path. This is a wholly different function from the small `Renderer.init(canvas)` that boots the 2D context — both happen to be named `init`, but this is the GPU one, and the larger of the two.

render.name: render()
render.desc:
`render(dw, dh, lightView, invView, count, fill, timeMs)` is PlanetGL's per-frame GPU draw. It takes the projected planet data `frame` has prepared and draws the lit spheres with WebGL2: it grows the instance buffers if the node count has risen, sizes the offscreen framebuffers to the viewport, draws the planets into them through `drawPlanets`, and runs the glow and blur passes that give the bodies their soft bloom before compositing.

It is the boundary between the CPU side, which decides *what* and *where*, and the GPU side, which decides *how it looks* — and it bails early if the WebGL context is not ready, letting the flat sprite path stand in.

link2.name: link2()
link2.desc: `link2(vsS, fsS)` compiles a vertex and a fragment shader through `sh` and links them into a WebGL program, returning null if either step fails. It is the small factory every shader program in the renderer is built with.

init_labels.name: initLabels()
init_labels.desc: `initLabels()` sets up the text-label pipeline on the GPU: it links a dedicated shader program (via `link2`) and its vertex array for drawing label quads, so node names can be rendered as textured billboards instead of slow DOM text. It is part of PlanetGL's one-time initialisation.

label_tex.name: labelTex()
label_tex.desc: `labelTex(key, w, h, drawFn)` returns a cached GPU texture for a piece of label text. If a texture for that key and size already exists it is reused; otherwise `drawFn` renders the text to an offscreen canvas and it is uploaded. Caching by key is what keeps labels cheap — a name is rasterised once and then drawn as a texture on every frame it is visible.

draw_labels.name: drawLabels()
draw_labels.desc: `drawLabels(items, dw, dh)` renders the frame's batch of visible node labels as textured quads through the label shader, blended over the scene. It runs late in the frame, after the bodies, so labels sit on top; each label's texture is supplied by `labelTex`.

build_stars.name: buildStars()
build_stars.desc: `buildStars()` bakes a small tileable star texture — an offscreen canvas of scattered points at varied brightness — used to fill the sky cheaply. Generating it once and tiling it is far cheaper than placing thousands of individual stars on every frame.

make_cloud_sprite.name: makeCloudSprite()
make_cloud_sprite.desc: `makeCloudSprite(col, seedv)` builds a structured dust-cloud sprite: bright additive wisps carved by dark dust lanes, seeded so it is reproducible. These are the sprites `buildGalaxy` scatters to give the galaxy its cloudy, nebular texture rather than a clean starfield.

build_galaxy.name: buildGalaxy()
build_galaxy.desc:
`buildGalaxy()` bakes the static galaxy backdrop *once*, not every frame. Using a fixed seed for reproducibility, it generates the star sphere, the band glow, the dust clouds and the background motes that give the sense of a galaxy surrounding the graph. Because these are expensive to build and do not change frame to frame, they are computed here and then simply swept by the camera while rendering.

It re-runs on events that change the backdrop's scale, and it seeds its randomness deterministically so the same galaxy looks the same every load rather than reshuffling its stars.

init.name: init() — Renderer
init.desc:
`init(canvas)` is the **Renderer**'s bootstrap. It stores the `#stage` input surface, bakes the reusable galaxy assets (`buildStars`, `buildGalaxy`), boots the WebGL layer through `PlanetGL.init`, and sizes everything with `resize` — the small orchestrator that stands the whole rendering stack up.

It is a different function from `init() — PlanetGL`: this one owns the scene and drives PlanetGL each frame, while PlanetGL owns the GPU and draws every pixel of the galaxy.
init.code: function init(canvas){ cv=canvas; buildStars(); buildGalaxy(); PlanetGL.init(); PlanetGL.uploadClouds(cloudSprites); resize(); }

glcol.name: glcol()
glcol.desc: `glcol(name)` converts a palette colour name into the pair of normalised RGB triples the planet shader expects — a base and a highlight — and caches the result. It is the small bridge between the app's named colours and the floats WebGL needs, memoised so each colour is converted only once.

resize.name: resize()
resize.desc: `resize()` fits the canvas to the window: it chooses a device-pixel ratio, sizes the canvas backing store and its CSS size, sets the drawing transform, and rebakes the resolution-dependent backdrop. It runs on load and whenever the window changes, keeping the render crisp on high-DPI screens without over-drawing.

refresh.name: refresh()
refresh.desc: `refresh()` is Renderer.refresh: it rebuilds the per-node colour-index array the renderer uses to choose each body's colour, by resolving every node's colour name to its palette slot. It runs when the data or grouping changes — after a load or an edit — so the drawn colours stay in step with the model.

ensure.name: ensure()
ensure.desc: `ensure(n)` makes sure the projection buffers — the typed arrays holding each node's screen x and y, radius, visibility and sort order — are sized for `n` nodes, reallocating only when the count changes. `frame` calls it first each tick so the rest of the pipeline can safely write into buffers it knows are the right size.
ensure.code:
function ensure(n){ if(proj.x.length!==n){ proj.x=new Float32Array(n); proj.y=new Float32Array(n);
    proj.r=new Float32Array(n); proj.az=new Float32Array(n); proj.vis=new Uint8Array(n); proj.front=new Uint8Array(n); order=new Int32Array(n); } }

frame.name: frame()
frame.desc:
`frame(view)` is the render loop's workhorse — the one function that draws a complete frame of the galaxy, called every tick by `loop`. It is by far the largest function in the codebase because it runs the whole visual pipeline in order: it sizes the projection buffers to the node count, rebuilds the solar topology if a node was added or removed, projects every node from 3D into screen space under the current camera and galaxy rotation, culls what is off-screen, then draws the backdrop, the connector lines, the glows and coronas, the lit planet bodies (handing the spheres to PlanetGL), the focus highlights, and finally the text labels.

It is deliberately monolithic. The per-frame state — projected positions, visibility, sort order, timing — is shared across every one of those stages, and threading it through separate functions would cost both clarity and speed on a path that runs many times a second. It reads the camera, focus and model but never mutates the model, so a frame is a pure snapshot of how things currently are, not a place where they change.

pick.name: pick()
pick.desc:
`pick(mx,my)` is the core hit-test: given a screen point it answers *which planet is under the pointer*. It runs in two passes. First it looks for a planet whose actual projected disc the point falls inside, and among those chooses the one nearest the camera — so a small planet drifting in front can't steal a click meant for the body you are literally pointing at. If nothing is directly hit, a second pass finds the closest planet within a small tolerance, so near-misses still land.

Almost every interaction begins here: focusing, selecting, dragging and connecting all start by asking `pick` what the user meant. Getting its priority right — disc-hit before proximity — is what makes tapping in a dense 3D cluster feel predictable rather than arbitrary.

pick_connector.name: pickConnector()
pick_connector.desc: `pickConnector(mx,my)` finds which connector *line* the pointer is near, within the currently focused system. It only runs in ego mode: it walks the visible connectors radiating from the system centre and returns the nearest one within a touch-friendly tolerance. This is how you tap a relationship — rather than a node — to inspect or edit that specific link, which is essential when the interesting thing is the tie between two bodies, not the bodies themselves.

pick_any_connector.name: pickAnyConnector()
pick_any_connector.desc: `pickAnyConnector(mx,my)` is the galaxy-wide counterpart to `pickConnector`: it finds the nearest connector line to a tap across *every* edge in the graph, not just those in the focused system. It exists so relationships remain selectable even when you are not inside a single system, letting you reach for a connection anywhere in the view.

center_dia.name: centerDia()
center_dia.desc: `centerDia()` returns the on-screen *diameter* of the focused system's centre — twice its projected radius — or 0 when it is not visible. It is a compact measure of how large the focused body appears right now, used when the view needs to be sized around it.
center_dia.code: function centerDia(){ const ec=Focus.egoCenter; return (ec>=0 && proj.vis && proj.vis[ec]) ? proj.r[ec]*2 : 0; }

center_screen.name: centerScreen()
center_screen.desc: `centerScreen()` reports where the focused system's centre — the ego sun — currently sits on screen, returning its projected x, y and radius, or `null` when that centre is not visible. Framing and layout code use it to anchor the view on the system you are actually exploring rather than on abstract world coordinates, so the thing you care about stays where you expect it.
center_screen.code: function centerScreen(){ const ec=Focus.egoCenter; return (ec>=0 && proj.vis && proj.vis[ec]) ? {x:proj.x[ec], y:proj.y[ec], r:proj.r[ec]} : null; }

clamp.name: clamp()
clamp.desc: `clamp(a,b,v)` keeps a value within the range `[a,b]` — the plainest of utilities, returning `a` or `b` when `v` strays past either. It appears throughout the camera and interaction code wherever a limit must be respected: zoom distance, slider positions, easing factors. It sits near the base of the codebase precisely because so much else depends on staying inside bounds.

seg_dist.name: segDist()
seg_dist.desc: `segDist(px,py, ax,ay, bx,by)` returns the shortest distance from a point to a line segment. It projects the point onto the segment, clamps the projection to the segment's endpoints so it never measures past the ends, and returns the remaining gap. It is the small, exact piece of geometry the connector-picking functions lean on to decide how close a tap falls to a relationship line.

universe_fit_dist.name: universeFitDist()
universe_fit_dist.desc: `universeFitDist()` computes the camera distance required to frame the entire galaxy. When the galaxy's overall radius is known it derives the distance from that disc and the viewport size; otherwise it falls back to measuring the spread of all the nodes. It is the number `flyOut` and the galaxy button reach for when pulling back so the whole structure fits — the exact counterpart to zooming into a single system.

fly_out.name: flyOut()
fly_out.desc: `flyOut()` aims the camera at the whole galaxy: it sets the view's target centre to the origin and its target distance to `universeFitDist`, and clears any fly target. It does not snap — it sets the goal the camera then eases toward — so the effect is a smooth pull-back from wherever you are to a view of the entire structure. It is the *show me everything* gesture.
fly_out.code: function flyOut(){ view.tcx=0; view.tcy=0; view.tcz=0; view.tdist=universeFitDist(); maxZoomDist=Math.max(R*3, view.tdist*1.15); view.flyTarget=-1; }

save_root.name: saveRoot()
save_root.desc: `saveRoot()` persists the root graph to local storage and marks the graph dirty, so the replace-guard knows there are changes to protect. It is called after edits, so your work survives a reload without any explicit save — the app autosaves to the browser.

group_of.name: groupOf()
group_of.desc: `groupOf(id)` returns a node's group id, or an empty string if it has none. A tiny accessor used by the visibility and colour logic so callers do not each reach into the model.

is_visible.name: isVisible()
is_visible.desc: `isVisible(id)` answers whether a node should be shown — true unless its group is currently hidden. It is the small predicate behind group toggling, consulted wherever hidden nodes must be filtered out: neighbours, picking, layout.

rebuild_vis.name: rebuildVis()
rebuild_vis.desc: `rebuildVis()` recomputes the per-node visibility flags from the set of hidden groups, so the renderer can cheaply skip nodes whose group is toggled off. It runs whenever group visibility changes, turning the `hiddenGroups` set into the fast per-index flags the frame path reads.
rebuild_vis.code: function rebuildVis(){ const n=Model.count(), ids=Model.ids; visFlags=new Uint8Array(n); for(let i=0;i<n;i++) visFlags[i]=isVisible(ids[i])?1:0; }

legend_entries.name: legendEntries()
legend_entries.desc: `legendEntries()` computes the legend's rows from the model's groups — each group's key, label and colour — in a stable order. It is the shared source both `buildLegend` and `buildTopbarLegend` render, so the two legends always agree.

paint_legend_into.name: paintLegendInto()
paint_legend_into.desc: `paintLegendInto(elId)` fills a legend element with one swatch-and-label chip per group, each toggling that group's visibility on tap and dimming when the group is hidden. It is the shared painter behind both legends — `buildLegend` calls it for the main HUD legend and again for the compact top-bar legend — so the two never drift apart.

build_legend.name: buildLegend()
build_legend.desc: `buildLegend()` builds both legends — the main HUD legend and the compact top-bar one — by calling the shared `paintLegendInto` for each. Every legend shows one colour swatch per group, and tapping a swatch toggles that group's visibility. It is rebuilt whenever the groups change.

build_topbar_legend.name: buildTopbarLegend()
build_topbar_legend.desc: `buildTopbarLegend()` paints just the compact top-bar legend, shown in focus mode, through `paintLegendInto`. It is the top-bar counterpart to the main legend; both draw the same group swatches through the shared painter.

sync_topbar.name: syncTopbar()
sync_topbar.desc: `syncTopbar()` keeps the top bar in step with the current mode: it shows the bar in focus mode with the focused node's title and a compact legend, and hides it in free-roam. It is called on every focus transition so the top bar always reflects where you are.

toggle_group.name: toggleGroup()
toggle_group.desc: `toggleGroup(k)` toggles a group's visibility on or off, with one safeguard: it refuses to hide the last visible group, so the entire galaxy can never be blanked. After toggling it rebuilds the visibility flags so the change takes effect. It is the action behind tapping a legend swatch.

esc.name: esc()
esc.desc: `esc(s)` escapes a string for safe insertion into HTML, replacing `&`, `<`, `>` and `"` with their entities. It is the ubiquitous guard against markup injection and broken layout: every card and panel builder runs user text through it before dropping it into `innerHTML`.

md.name: md()
md.desc:
`md(s)` is a small Markdown renderer that turns a node's description into HTML — handling fenced code blocks, links, emphasis and line breaks, while escaping everything else so raw text stays safe. Code blocks are pulled out first and restored last, so their contents are not mangled by the inline rules.

It is what lets descriptions carry light formatting — and, in this codebase graph, the reason the explanations you are reading render with paragraphs and inline code rather than as flat text.

open_vid_lb.name: openVidLB()
open_vid_lb.desc: `openVidLB(embed)` opens the video lightbox with an embedded player, dropping an iframe for the given video into the overlay box. Used for inline video that plays in place rather than opening the full web view.

close_vid_lb.name: closeVidLB()
close_vid_lb.desc: `closeVidLB()` closes the video lightbox and stops playback by clearing the embed, so nothing keeps playing behind the scenes. The counterpart to `openVidLB`.
close_vid_lb.code: function closeVidLB(){ const lb=document.getElementById("vidlb"); if(!lb||lb.style.display==="none") return; lb.style.display="none"; document.getElementById("vidlb-box").innerHTML=""; }

open_lightbox.name: openLightbox()
open_lightbox.desc: `openLightbox(im)` opens the image lightbox for a tapped picture, animating it up from where it sits to a large centred view. It reads the full-resolution source if one is provided, fades in the backdrop, and eases the image into place. It is the app's way of letting node images be inspected without leaving the graph; `closeLightbox` reverses it.

close_lightbox.name: closeLightbox()
close_lightbox.desc: `closeLightbox()` dismisses the image lightbox, fading the backdrop out and shrinking the image back toward where it came from. The reverse of `openLightbox`.

yt_embed.name: ytEmbed()
yt_embed.desc: `ytEmbed(u)` recognises a YouTube reference — a bare 11-character id or any of the common URL forms — and returns the corresponding privacy-friendly embed URL, or null if it is not YouTube. It is the small parser behind `videoBlock` and `openVideo`.

video_block.name: videoBlock()
video_block.desc: `videoBlock(url, c)` is the single, consistent video renderer used everywhere a node or card has a video: it produces an embedded player for YouTube (privacy-friendly nocookie, fullscreen-capable) or a link-out for other URLs. Centralising it means every video across the app looks and behaves the same.

open_video.name: openVideo()
open_video.desc: `openVideo(url)` opens a video for viewing: if it recognises a YouTube link it builds the embed and opens it in the web view with autoplay, otherwise it opens the URL directly. It is the single entry point behind a video affordance on a card.
open_video.code: function openVideo(url){ const emb=ytEmbed(url); if(emb) openWebview(emb+"?autoplay=1&rel=0","Video"); else openWebview(url,"Video"); }

open_webview.name: openWebview()
open_webview.desc: `openWebview(url, title)` opens the embedded web view — an in-app iframe panel — pointed at a URL, with a title and an external-open link. It is how weblinks and videos are shown inside the app rather than navigating away; `closeWebview` dismisses it.

close_webview.name: closeWebview()
close_webview.desc: `closeWebview()` closes the embedded web view, fading it out and clearing the iframe so nothing keeps loading or playing. The counterpart to `openWebview`.

ramp.name: ramp()
ramp.desc: `ramp(id)` returns the full palette entry — the set of shades — for a node's colour, by resolving its group's colour name and looking it up in the palette. It is the colour accessor the card and render code reach for whenever they need a node's tints: a one-liner over `colorName` and the palette.

neighbours_of.name: neighboursOf()
neighbours_of.desc:
`neighboursOf(id)` collects a node's immediate connections into a tidy list — each entry recording the neighbour, the relationship text, and the direction of the tie — de-duplicating so a node appears once even if linked several times. It reads only the model's real links now, the transient staging links of the old drag-to-connect flow having been removed.

It is the function that turns raw edges into the ring of planets around a focused sun: navigation and card code call it to learn who orbits a node, and how.

to_edge.name: toEdge()
to_edge.desc: `toEdge(ox, oy, tx, ty, hw, hh)` returns the point on the edge of a rectangle — centred at `ox,oy`, half-size `hw,hh` — along the line toward a target, clamped so it never overshoots the target. It is what lets connector lines meet a card at its border instead of disappearing into its middle, used in the frame's connector routing.

attach_card_drag.name: attachCardDrag()
attach_card_drag.desc: `attachCardDrag(card, nid, k)` wires the pointer-drag behaviour onto a neighbour card so it can be repositioned within the focus constellation, pinned where you drop it. The old connect-by-dragging mode has been removed — dragging now only moves a card; connections are made in the editor's Connections section instead.

make_focus_card_html.name: makeFocusCardHtml()
make_focus_card_html.desc:
`makeFocusCardHtml(nd, c, nm, orb)` builds the inner markup for the *central* card in focus mode — the node you are studying. It lays out the large orb or avatar, the name, the group tint, the description, and the action affordances: hide-focus, weblink, video, portrait and enter-subgraph. It sizes itself against the viewport so it reads well on both phone and desktop.

It is one of the two branches split out of `makeCard`, called when the card being built is the focus node. It returns HTML carrying only class names — the look itself lives in the CSS component styles.

make_neighbour_card_html.name: makeNeighbourCardHtml()
make_neighbour_card_html.desc: `makeNeighbourCardHtml(nd, c, nm, orb, id, rel, showAvatar)` builds the inner markup for a neighbour card — one of the bodies ringing the focused node: a compact orb, the node name, and the relationship label describing how it ties to the focus. It returns HTML with class names only, leaving styling to the CSS. The brought-in glow and inline-rename affordances of the old drag-to-connect flow have been removed.

make_card.name: makeCard()
make_card.desc: `makeCard(id, isFocus, rel, showAvatar)` builds one 2D card element for a node in focus mode: it creates the element and its orb, then delegates the inner markup to `makeFocusCardHtml` for the centre card or `makeNeighbourCardHtml` for a ring neighbour, and wires the dismiss and add-node handlers. It is called for the centre card and every neighbour in the constellation.

build_focus_center_card.name: buildFocusCenterCard()
build_focus_center_card.desc: `buildFocusCenterCard(host, CX, CY)` creates and wires the central focus card: it builds the card with `makeCard`, centres it, and attaches its interactions — the hide-focus button, double-tap and long-press to open the editor, and a pointer drag that rotates the whole view. (The drag's old connect-line mode is gone.) It was split out of `buildFocusCards` so the wiring lives apart from the layout maths.

build_focus_cards.name: buildFocusCards()
build_focus_cards.desc: `buildFocusCards()` lays out the focus-mode card constellation — the focused node ringed by a card per neighbour. It delegates the central card and its wiring to `buildFocusCenterCard`, builds a neighbour card per connected node with `makeCard`, then distributes them evenly around a rounded, inset boundary (via the nested `_rr`), relaxes overlaps, and routes a connector line from each back to the centre before animating them into place.

rr.name: _rr()
rr.desc:
`_rr(s)` maps a distance `s` travelled along the perimeter of the layout's rounded rectangle to an actual point on that perimeter, working out which straight edge or rounded corner the distance falls on and returning the coordinate there.

It is the geometric core of `buildFocusCards`'s neighbour placement: by stepping evenly in arc-length and calling `_rr` at each step, the layout spreads the neighbour cards uniformly around the rounded, inset boundary instead of bunching them at the corners. It is a nested helper defined inside `buildFocusCards`.

enter_focus.name: enterFocus()
enter_focus.desc: `enterFocus(id)` enters focus mode on a node — the 2D card view where the node is ringed by its neighbours. It sets the focus state, builds the constellation, shows the top bar and the focus-only controls (including the add-node + and new-connection ⊸ buttons), and hides the free-roam controls. It is the main way into the 2D view.

exit_focus.name: exitFocus()
exit_focus.desc: `exitFocus()` leaves focus mode back to the galaxy: it clears the focus state, hides the top bar and focus-only controls, and restores the free-roam navigation controls — while now keeping the add-node + button available in the galaxy too, so you are never stranded without a way to add a node. The counterpart to `enterFocus`.

ego_spike.name: egoSpike()
ego_spike.desc:
`egoSpike(id)` performs the visual *arrival* when you drop into a node's system. It clears any planet sub-focus, wipes the 2D card layer, dismisses the relations panel, and positions the add-node affordance, then reconciles the camera framing, zoom slider and top bar to the new system.

It is the moment-of-transition housekeeping that leaves the ego view clean and ready — deliberately separate from the state changes `egoTo` makes, so the *what am I looking at* and the *how does it look* are handled in distinct steps.

rel_detail_gen.name: relDetailGen()
rel_detail_gen.desc: `relDetailGen(type, a, b)` writes a readable sentence for a connection that has no explicit description, from its connector type and the two node names — turning, say, a *parent* link between A and B into `A is a parent of B`. It is the fallback that keeps every relationship legible even when the author never wrote a custom line, and it is exactly what `linkDetails` and `linkDetailsAll` reach for when a link's own text is missing.
rel_detail_gen.code:
function relDetailGen(type, a, b){
  const T={parent:a+" is a parent of "+b+" — a tie of blood and lineage.",
    consort:a+" and "+b+" are consorts, bound as partners.",
    kills:a+" slays "+b+" — a fatal, defining act between them.",
    protects:a+" stands as protector of "+b+", shielding them from harm.",
    sibling:a+" and "+b+" are siblings, sprung from a shared line.",
    endangers:a+" is a peril to "+b+", a threat of ruin.",
    captivates:a+" holds "+b+" captive.",
    loves:a+" loves "+b+", a longing that shapes them both.",
    advises:a+" counsels "+b+", guiding their course.",
    rival:a+" and "+b+" are rivals, locked in contest.",
    companion:a+" and "+b+" travel together as companions.",
    serves:a+" serves "+b+".",
    mentors:a+" mentors "+b+", shaping their path.",
    hosts:a+" gives "+b+" hospitality.",
    forges:a+" forges wonders for "+b+".",
    wounds:a+" wounds "+b+".",
    transforms:a+" transforms "+b+".",
    friend:a+" and "+b+" are friends, loyal to one another.",
    courts:a+" courts "+b+"."};
  return T[type] || (a+" and "+b+" share a "+type+" bond.");
}

link_details.name: linkDetails()
link_details.desc: `linkDetails(aId, bId)` returns the first connection between two nodes, or null — a thin wrapper over `linkDetailsAll(aId, bId)[0]`. Used where only one representative tie is needed.

link_details_all.name: linkDetailsAll()
link_details_all.desc: `linkDetailsAll(aId, bId)` returns every connection between two nodes, each with its type, direction and text, reading the model's real links (the old transient staging links are gone). Because two nodes can be tied more than once, it returns them all; `linkDetails` takes the first.

focus_planet.name: focusPlanet()
focus_planet.desc:
`focusPlanet(i)` narrows attention from a whole system down to one planet within it. It pins that planet and frames it *once* so the entire planet fits at a consistent size — the same framing for every planet, so none feels arbitrarily larger — and records the visit as a breadcrumb stop.

This is the second level of focus: from *this system* to *this one relationship*. It is what surfaces a planet's relationship card, letting you read exactly how that body relates to the sun at the centre.

go_to_node.name: goToNode()
go_to_node.desc:
`goToNode(i)` is the router for a clicked node — it decides what *going to* that node should actually mean, so a tap always lands somewhere coherent. If the node is a sun (or the graph has no sun structure yet), it simply travels there via `egoTo`. If the node is a planet, it first jumps to that planet's *sun's* system — so all the planet's siblings are in orbit around you — and then focuses the planet in place.

That two-case rule is the quiet logic that makes clicking feel right: tap a hub and you enter its system; tap a satellite and you are taken to where that satellite lives and shown it in context, rather than ripped out of its surroundings.

ego_to.name: egoTo()
ego_to.desc:
`egoTo(id)` is the fuller *go and live in this node's system* action. It does something `enterFocus` does not: it **promotes** the node first, turning it into a sun so its neighbours are physically pulled across to orbit it. Only then does it record the focus, collect the visible neighbours, and run `egoSpike` to set up the ego view.

So where `enterFocus` establishes focus *state*, `egoTo` also reshapes the galaxy so the chosen node genuinely becomes the centre of its own system — which is what lets any node, not just an original hub, be explored as one. It also drops a breadcrumb, so the trail back through your exploration is preserved.

show_rel_info_edge.name: showRelInfoEdge()
show_rel_info_edge.desc: `showRelInfoEdge(a, b, px, py)` shows the relations panel for a specific edge between two nodes — the detail of that one connection. The edge-targeted counterpart to `showRelInfo`.

hide_rel_info.name: hideRelInfo()
hide_rel_info.desc: `hideRelInfo()` hides the relations panel — the small popup listing a node's ties. A dismiss used when navigating away.
hide_rel_info.code: function hideRelInfo(){ const box=document.getElementById("relinfo"); if(box) box.style.display="none"; }

pick_image_file.name: pickImageFile()
pick_image_file.desc: `pickImageFile(cb)` opens a file picker for an image and hands the chosen file to a callback. The shared entry point behind the icon and image upload controls in the editor.
pick_image_file.code:
function pickImageFile(cb){ const inp=document.createElement("input"); inp.type="file"; inp.accept="image/*"; inp.style.display="none"; document.body.appendChild(inp);
  inp.onchange=function(){ const f=this.files&&this.files[0]; if(f){ const r=new FileReader(); r.onload=()=>{ cb(r.result); inp.remove(); }; r.readAsDataURL(f); } else inp.remove(); }; inp.click(); }

size_card_edit.name: sizeCardEdit()
size_card_edit.desc: `sizeCardEdit()` sizes the inline editor box to fit its content within the viewport while editing — a small layout helper that keeps the in-place editor readable on any screen.
size_card_edit.code: function sizeCardEdit(){ const box=document.getElementById("planetinfo"); if(!box||!cardEditing) return; const vv=window.visualViewport, vh=vv?vv.height:innerHeight; box.style.maxHeight=Math.max(160, vh-150)+"px"; box.style.overflowY="auto"; }

exit_card_edit.name: exitCardEdit()
exit_card_edit.desc:
`exitCardEdit()` handles a Done or close of the inline editor, enforcing two rules first. A node must have a name: if it is blank, an inline warning appears at the top of the box offering Discard or Keep editing rather than closing. And any connection filled in but not yet added in the Connections section is committed automatically (via `_editConnectCommit`).

Then it tears the editor down through `_reallyExitCardEdit` and, for a freshly created node, pulls it into the current view — a neighbour card in the 2D focus view, or navigating to it in the 3D galaxy.

really_exit_card_edit.name: _reallyExitCardEdit()
really_exit_card_edit.desc: `_reallyExitCardEdit()` performs the actual teardown of the inline editor: it clears the edit state, removes the `card-editing` body class so the CSS restores the hidden controls, resets the info box's sizing, and returns it to read-only. It is split out of `exitCardEdit` so the name-required guard can decide *whether* to close — warning first on a nameless node — while this function owns the closing itself.
really_exit_card_edit.code: function _reallyExitCardEdit(){ cardEditing=false; _editKind=null; _editNode=null; _editNodeId=null; _newNodeId=null; _editConnectCommit=null; try{ document.body.classList.remove("card-editing"); }catch(_){} try{document.activeElement&&document.activeElement.blur();}catch(_){} const box=document.getElementById("planetinfo"); if(box){ box.style.top=""; box.style.bottom=""; box.style.maxHeight=""; box.style.textAlign=""; box.style.width=""; if(Focus.mode!=="ego") box.style.display="none"; } planetInfoShown=null; }

build_edit_highlight.name: buildEditHighlight()
build_edit_highlight.desc: `buildEditHighlight(box, target)` builds the highlight toggle in the inline editor — a control to add the node or connection to the current highlight set. A small section builder used by `enterCardEdit`.

build_edit_start.name: buildEditStart()
build_edit_start.desc: `buildEditStart(spec, box)` builds the 'set as start node' control in the inline editor, marking which node a fresh load of the document should open on. A section builder for `enterCardEdit`.

build_edit_link_type.name: buildEditLinkType()
build_edit_link_type.desc: `buildEditLinkType(box, target)` builds the connector-type section of the inline editor when a connection is being edited: a selector to change the link's type, and the means to define a new type inline. It lets you re-label how two nodes relate without leaving the card.

build_edit_delete_conn.name: buildEditDeleteConn()
build_edit_delete_conn.desc: `buildEditDeleteConn(box, target)` builds the delete-connection control in the inline editor, splicing the link out of the model on confirmation. The connection counterpart to `buildEditDeleteNode`.

build_edit_node_fields.name: buildEditNodeFields()
build_edit_node_fields.desc: `buildEditNodeFields(box, target)` builds the node-field section of the inline editor: the name, description, group selector, icon and image controls, and media and weblink fields for the node being edited. Each field writes straight back to the node as you change it. One of the section builders `enterCardEdit` assembles.

build_edit_delete_node.name: buildEditDeleteNode()
build_edit_delete_node.desc: `buildEditDeleteNode(spec, box)` builds the delete-node control in the inline editor: a two-tap confirm that removes the node and its links from the model and rebuilds the view. Kept as its own section so the destructive action stays deliberate.

code_preview.name: codePreview()
code_preview.desc: `codePreview(code, dataAttr, accent)` returns a compact preview of a code block: the first few lines in a bordered monospace box with a fade-out and a tap-to-expand footer that opens the full text in `openCodeBox`. It appears on cards whose node or connection carries a `code` field — including every function node in this graph.

open_code_box.name: openCodeBox()
open_code_box.desc:
`openCodeBox(code, onSave, title)` opens the full-screen code lightbox: a scrollable, monospace panel that preserves whitespace. Given a save callback it acts as an editor; without one it is a read-only viewer. It is the shared surface for the `code` field, reached from the inline editor's add-code button, from a card's code preview, and from the connection builder.

It creates the overlay on first use and reuses it thereafter, so opening code is cheap however often you do it.

build_edit_code.name: buildEditCode()
build_edit_code.desc: `buildEditCode(box, target, label)` builds the 'Code Block' row of the inline editor — an add/edit-code button that opens the code lightbox (`openCodeBox`) and stores the text on the node's or connection's `code` field, clearing it when left blank. It sits just below Description, and is shown for both node and connection editors.

build_edit_connect.name: buildEditConnect()
build_edit_connect.desc:
`buildEditConnect(box, thisId)` builds the Connections section of the inline node editor — the in-place way to link the node you're editing to another. It lists the node's existing connections (each removable), then offers a target-node dropdown (defaulting to the focused node), a connector-type dropdown with an inline create-new-type option, and an Add button.

It exposes its commit logic as `_editConnectCommit` so pressing Done finalises a filled-but-not-added connection automatically. This section, with the new add-node flow, replaces the old drag-a-line-between-cards gesture: you now create a node and wire it up entirely from the editor.

enter_card_edit.name: enterCardEdit()
enter_card_edit.desc:
`enterCardEdit(spec)` is the single inline editor — the hold-to-edit box that appears when you long-press or double-tap a card, and the only editor the app now has. It turns the info box into a form for the target node or connection, in place.

It lays the fields out top-to-bottom — Name, Description, Code Block, then links and media, then Group, and finally the Connections section for nodes — assembling each from its own section builder (`buildEditNodeFields`, `buildEditConnect`, `buildEditCode`, and the rest). It is the orchestrator; each section owns its fields, and `exitCardEdit` closes it while enforcing the name requirement.

sync_i.name: syncI()
sync_i.desc: `sync_i()` is the icon-field counterpart of `sync`: it updates the icon controls' status to reflect whether an uploaded icon is in use.
sync_i.code: function syncI(){ if(isData()){ st.textContent="Uploaded in use"; rm.style.display=""; paste.style.display="none"; } else { st.textContent=""; rm.style.display=target[key]?"":"none"; paste.style.display=""; } }

stop_card_video.name: stopCardVideo()
stop_card_video.desc: `stopCardVideo()` stops any video playing inside the info card by clearing its embed — called when the card is rebuilt or dismissed, so audio does not keep playing off-screen.
stop_card_video.code: function stopCardVideo(){ const b=document.getElementById("planetinfo"); if(b && b.querySelector("iframe")){ b.innerHTML=""; planetInfoShown=null; } }

pi_sun_card_html.name: piSunCardHtml()
pi_sun_card_html.desc:
`piSunCardHtml(nd, c, id)` builds the HTML for a sun (hub) info card — what you see when a hub node is the centre of attention. It assembles the header with the node's name and coloured accent, its icon or image, the description rendered from markdown, any embedded media, and — for documents that carry code, like this one — a preview of the node's `code` block that expands into the full lightbox.

It was split out of `updatePlanetInfo` so the sun-card branch is a self-contained string builder rather than inline code on the frame path. `updatePlanetInfo` calls it and drops the returned markup into the info box.

pi_planet_card_html.name: piPlanetCardHtml()
pi_planet_card_html.desc:
`piPlanetCardHtml(nd, c, dets, lk, pid, sid, sn)` builds the HTML for a focused planet's *relationship* card — the planet together with the sun it orbits. It renders a header, then each connection between the two with its type label and direction, a preview of any per-connection `code`, and any media or weblinks. Because two nodes can be tied more than once, it lists every relationship rather than just one.

Like its sun-card sibling it was split out of `updatePlanetInfo`; the frame path hands it the pre-computed relationship details and it returns the finished card markup.

update_planet_info.name: updatePlanetInfo()
update_planet_info.desc:
`updatePlanetInfo()` is the per-frame owner of the info box. Every frame it decides what the box should show — a sun card, a focused-planet relationship card, or nothing — and cross-fades between them as the focus changes, so cards ease in and out rather than snapping. It yields entirely while an inline editor is open, letting editing own the box.

The card markup itself is delegated to `piSunCardHtml` and `piPlanetCardHtml`; this function handles the gating, the fade easing, the sizing that grows the card with zoom, and the lifecycle of any embedded card video. Because it runs on the frame path it rebuilds the card only when the focus actually changes, not on every tick.

hide_planet_info.name: hidePlanetInfo()
hide_planet_info.desc: `hidePlanetInfo()` hides the planet info card and clears the edit flag. A small dismiss used when focus changes or a card must be cleared.
hide_planet_info.code: function hidePlanetInfo(){ cardEditing=false; const box=document.getElementById("planetinfo"); if(box){ if(box.querySelector("iframe")) box.innerHTML=""; box.style.display="none"; box.style.opacity="1"; box.style.top=""; box.style.bottom=""; box.style.maxHeight=""; } planetInfoShown=null; }

add_temp_node.name: addTempNode()
add_temp_node.desc: `addTempNode()` is the add-node action behind the + button. It creates a fresh, un-named node — seeded near the focused node, or at the galaxy centre when nothing is focused, so it works in any view — and immediately opens the inline editor on it. You name it and, optionally, connect it there; on Done it becomes a proper node and is pulled into the current view. This replaced the old temporary-node-plus-drag-a-line flow.

start_name_edit.name: startNameEdit()
start_name_edit.desc: `startNameEdit(id, el)` turns a node's name into an editable field in place, so a node can be renamed directly on its card: it swaps the name for an input and writes the new value back to the model. The node-level counterpart to `startRename`, which renames the whole graph.

float_controls.name: floatControls()
float_controls.desc: `floatControls(show)` shows or hides the floating controls according to the current mode — and it is mode-aware rather than a blunt on/off. The navigation controls (zoom, spin, breadcrumb) hide in focus mode; the focus-only buttons follow the `show` flag; the connector and bypass toggles are repainted as they appear. It is called on every transition between free-roam and focus so the control surface always matches what you can do.

update_toggle_btn.name: updateToggleBtn()
update_toggle_btn.desc: `updateToggleBtn()` sets the focus/galaxy toggle to its 'see the whole galaxy' state — its glyph and tooltip — used while a focus is active so the button offers the way back out. A small paint helper for that one control.
update_toggle_btn.code:
function updateToggleBtn(){ const b=document.getElementById("togglefocus"); if(!b) return;
  b.innerHTML = "⊕"; b.title = "See the whole galaxy"; }

paint_breadcrumb_btn.name: paintBreadcrumbBtn()
paint_breadcrumb_btn.desc: `paintBreadcrumbBtn()` updates the breadcrumb toggle's look to reflect whether the breadcrumb trail is currently on — brightening it when active, dimming it when not. One of a small family of paint-* helpers that keep a toggle button's appearance in step with its state.
paint_breadcrumb_btn.code: function paintBreadcrumbBtn(){ const b=document.getElementById("breadcrumb"); if(!b) return; const on=Focus._breadcrumbOn; b.style.color=on?"var(--t1)":"var(--t3)"; b.style.opacity=on?"1":"0.5"; b.style.borderColor="var(--line-strong)"; b.style.background="var(--card)"; b.title=on?"Hide the trail of where you've been":"Show the trail of where you've been"; }

close_hl_list.name: closeHlList()
close_hl_list.desc: `closeHlList()` closes the highlights panel and clears the highlight-view flag — a small dismiss, the counterpart to opening the panel.
close_hl_list.code: function closeHlList(){ Focus._highlightView=false; const el=document.getElementById("hllist"); if(el) el.style.display="none"; if(Focus._paintHl) Focus._paintHl(); }

show_info_card.name: showInfoCard()
show_info_card.desc: `showInfoCard(msg, title)` pops a small transient message card — the app's lightweight way of telling you something (say, that a file has no nodes to merge) without a blocking dialog. It creates the card on first use and reuses it thereafter.
show_info_card.code:
function showInfoCard(msg, title){ let el=document.getElementById("infocard"); if(!el){ el=document.createElement("div"); el.id="infocard"; el.style.cssText="display:none; position:fixed; inset:0; z-index:2500; align-items:center; justify-content:center; background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5); pointer-events:auto; padding:20px; box-sizing:border-box;"; el.innerHTML='
'; document.body.appendChild(el); el.addEventListener("click", e=>{ if(e.target===el || e.target.classList.contains("ic-ok")) el.style.display="none"; }); } const _t=el.querySelector(".ic-title"); _t.textContent=title||"Xanadu"; _t.style.display=title?"block":"none"; el.querySelector(".ic-msg").textContent=msg; el.style.display="flex"; }

hl_promote_focused.name: hlPromoteFocused()
hl_promote_focused.desc: `hlPromoteFocused()` promotes the currently focused planet into a sun with the 'ignite' transition — capturing the planet's on-screen size first so the animation grows smoothly from where it sits rather than snapping. It is the action behind turning a planet you are looking at into the centre of its own system.
hl_promote_focused.code: function hlPromoteFocused(){ if(Focus.planetFocus>=0){ const pf=Focus.planetFocus; const id=Model.ids[pf]; Focus._igTargetScreenR=Focus._lastPlanetScreenR||0; Focus._igniteId=pf; Focus._igniteT0=performance.now(); Focus.planetFocus=-1; egoTo(id); if(Focus._lastPlanetScreenR>0.5){ const _sr=(SolarSys.sunR&&SolarSys.sunR[pf])||((SolarSys.Rmax||40)*1.2); view.dist=_sr*1150/(Focus._lastPlanetScreenR*7.5); } view.tdist=view.dist; Focus._igniteZoom=true; } }

hl_click_node.name: hlClickNode()
hl_click_node.desc: `hlClickNode(i)` handles a tap on a node row in the highlights list: it closes the list, travels to that node via `goToNode`, and then — once the camera has settled, through `hlAfterSettle` — fine-tunes the framing. It is how a highlighted node becomes a one-tap destination.
hl_click_node.code: function hlClickNode(i){ closeHlList(); const n=Model.count(); if(SolarSys.isSun && SolarSys.isSun.length===n && SolarSys.isSun[i]){ goToNode(i); hlAfterSettle(()=>{ view.tdist=(Focus.fitDist||view.dist)*0.55; }); } else { goToNode(i); Focus._hlAutoPromote=true; const _iv=setInterval(()=>{ if(typeof hideRelInfo==="function") hideRelInfo(); }, 40); hlAfterSettle(()=>{ view.dist=view.tdist; requestAnimationFrame(()=>{ hlPromoteFocused(); setTimeout(()=>{ clearInterval(_iv); Focus._hlAutoPromote=false; }, 1900); }); }); } }

hl_after_settle.name: hlAfterSettle()
hl_after_settle.desc: `hlAfterSettle(cb, timeout)` waits until the camera has essentially stopped — polling until the view distance is close to its target, or a timeout elapses — then runs the callback. It lets navigation steps that must happen *after* a fly finishes (a final reframing, say) fire at the right moment instead of mid-transition.
hl_after_settle.code: function hlAfterSettle(cb, timeout){ const t0=performance.now(); timeout=timeout||3800; let cnt=0; const iv=setInterval(()=>{ const near=view.tdist>0 && Math.abs(view.dist-view.tdist)<view.tdist*0.006; if(near) cnt++; else cnt=0; if(cnt>=8 || performance.now()-t0>timeout){ clearInterval(iv); cb(); } }, 60); }

hl_click_conn.name: hlClickConn()
hl_click_conn.desc: `hlClickConn(l)` handles a tap on a *connection* row in the highlights list: it resolves the two endpoints and navigates so that relationship is in view, jumping to the relevant system and framing the tie. The connection counterpart to `hlClickNode`.

build_hl_list.name: buildHlList()
build_hl_list.desc: `buildHlList()` builds the highlights panel — a list of the nodes and connections currently in the highlight set, with a title and a clickable row per entry. It is rebuilt whenever the highlight set changes; its rows route through `hlClickNode` and `hlClickConn` when tapped, so the panel doubles as a jump-to navigator.
build_hl_list.code: function buildHlList(){ const el=document.getElementById("hllist"); if(!el) return; el.innerHTML=""; const _ttl=document.createElement("div"); _ttl.className="hl-title"; _ttl.innerHTML='Highlights'; const _dis=document.createElement("button"); _dis.className="pf-dismiss"; _dis.title="Close"; _dis.innerHTML="\u2296"; _dis.style.cssText="width:26px;height:26px;border-radius:50%;background:var(--card);border:1px solid var(--line-strong);color:var(--t2);cursor:pointer;display:flex;align-items:center;justify-content:center;padding:0;font-size:14px;line-height:1;flex:none;"; _dis.onclick=(e)=>{ e.stopPropagation(); closeHlList(); }; _ttl.appendChild(_dis); el.appendChild(_ttl); const n=Model.count(); const items=[]; for(let i=0;ia.txt.localeCompare(b.txt)); items.forEach(it=>{ const lab=document.createElement("div"); lab.className="hllab"; const _id=(it.node!=null)?Model.ids[it.node]:null; const _cc=_id?ramp(_id):null; const _cb=(_cc&&_cc[2])||"#888"; if(_id){ lab.style.background=_cb; lab.style.color="#fff"; } const _grp=_id?(((Model.raw.groups||{})[groupOf(_id)]||{}).label||""):""; lab.style.display="flex"; lab.style.alignItems="center"; lab.innerHTML=''+esc(it.txt)+''+(_grp?''+esc(_grp)+'':''); if(it.node!=null){ lab.onclick=()=>hlClickNode(it.node); } else if(it.link){ lab.onclick=()=>hlClickConn(it.link); } el.appendChild(lab); }); }

paint_conn_btn.name: paintConnBtn()
paint_conn_btn.desc: `paintConnBtn()` updates the connector toggle's look to reflect whether connector lines are currently shown. The paint-half of the show-connections toggle.
paint_conn_btn.code:
function paintConnBtn(){ const b=document.getElementById("toggleconn"); if(!b) return; const on=view.showConnectors!==false;
  b.style.color=on?"var(--t1)":"var(--t3)"; b.style.opacity=on?"1":"0.5"; b.title=on?"Hide connector lines":"Show connector lines"; }

paint_bypass_btn.name: paintBypassBtn()
paint_bypass_btn.desc: `paintBypassBtn()` updates the bypass-storage button's look to reflect whether the saved-graph bypass is on — an admin/test toggle that ignores the locally saved graph. Like its siblings it only repaints; the state itself lives elsewhere.

slider_from_zoom.name: sliderFromZoom()
slider_from_zoom.desc: `sliderFromZoom(dist)` converts a camera distance into a zoom-slider position, applying a square-root curve so the slider feels even across a wide range of distances. It is the inverse of `zoomFromSlider`, used to keep the slider in step with the camera.
slider_from_zoom.code: function sliderFromZoom(dist){ const ZO=Math.max(ZIN+1,maxZoomDist); const f=Math.sqrt(Math.max(0,Math.min(1,(ZO-dist)/(ZO-ZIN)))); return Math.round(f*100); }

zoom_from_slider.name: zoomFromSlider()
zoom_from_slider.desc: `zoomFromSlider(v)` converts a zoom-slider position into a camera distance, applying a squared curve so dragging the slider maps naturally onto the large range of zoom. The inverse of `sliderFromZoom`; together they keep slider and camera consistent in both directions.
zoom_from_slider.code: function zoomFromSlider(v){ const ZO=Math.max(ZIN+1,maxZoomDist); const f=v/100; return ZO+(ZIN-ZO)*(f*f); }

sync_zoom_slider.name: syncZoomSlider()
sync_zoom_slider.desc: `syncZoomSlider()` sets the zoom slider to match the current camera distance — through `sliderFromZoom` — unless the user is actively dragging it. It is how the slider tracks the camera when zoom changes by other means, without fighting the user's own drag.
sync_zoom_slider.code: function syncZoomSlider(){ const zs=document.getElementById("zoomslider"); if(zs && !zoomSliderActive) zs.value=sliderFromZoom(view.tdist); }

paint_hide_btn.name: paintHideBtn()
paint_hide_btn.desc: `paintHideBtn()` updates the hide-unconnected button's look to reflect whether unconnected nodes are currently hidden. The paint-half of that toggle, called by `setHideUnconnected`.

set_hide_unconnected.name: setHideUnconnected()
set_hide_unconnected.desc: `setHideUnconnected(v)` sets whether unconnected nodes are hidden and repaints the toggle through `paintHideBtn`. The state-setting half of that option, kept separate from the button that shows it.

enter_subgraph.name: enterSubgraph()
enter_subgraph.desc: `enterSubgraph(nodeId)` descends into a node's nested subgraph — a graph attached to a node — by pushing the current document onto the graph stack and loading the child. It is what turns a node into a doorway to a whole other galaxy, with the breadcrumb trail recording the path down so you can climb back out.

exit_to_level.name: exitToLevel()
exit_to_level.desc: `exitToLevel(i)` climbs back up the graph stack to a chosen depth, discards the deeper documents, reloads the ancestor, and then **frames the return by the kind of node you came from**: a sun re-centres on it (`egoTo`); a connection *planet* egos onto its parent sun and sets `planetFocus` to the planet — so you land looking at the connection in its system rather than zoomed onto the sun — clearing any stray ignite; otherwise it restores the saved camera. It is the landing half of the return journey, paired with `enterSubgraphDoc`, and is reached both from the breadcrumb and from `exitPortal`.

render_graph_trail.name: renderGraphTrail()
render_graph_trail.desc: `renderGraphTrail()` renders the breadcrumb trail of nested graphs — one crumb per level of the graph stack, from the root document down to where you are now — each clickable to climb back to that level. It keeps the trail in step as you descend into subgraphs and back out, and toggles the export-view control alongside it.

show_loading.name: showLoading()
show_loading.desc: `showLoading(pct)` shows the loading overlay and updates its progress text and bar to `pct`. It is driven by the streaming layout simulation as it settles, giving feedback on first load; `hideLoading` clears it when the layout has cooled.

hide_loading.name: hideLoading()
hide_loading.desc: `hideLoading()` hides the loading overlay and cancels its timer. Called once the initial layout has settled, it clears the progress screen that the streaming simulation showed.

build_solar_topology.name: buildSolarTopology()
build_solar_topology.desc:
`buildSolarTopology()` decides the fundamental shape of the galaxy: which nodes are suns and which orbit them as planets. It computes each node's degree — how many connections it has — then sets the sun threshold at the 80th-percentile degree (never lower than 3). Nodes above the line become suns; everything else becomes a planet of the sun it links to most strongly.

The output is the solar-system membership map — which planets belong to which sun — that every later stage builds on. It re-runs whenever the topology could have changed (a load, an edit, a promotion), keeping the sun/planet structure honest to the current graph. This is the step that gives Xanadu its defining metaphor.

build_solar_orbits.name: buildSolarOrbits()
build_solar_orbits.desc:
`buildSolarOrbits(keep)` turns the abstract sun/planet membership into concrete positions. It lays the suns along a spiral with the biggest hubs drawn toward the bright core, then assigns each planet an orbit around its sun — radius and angle chosen so the systems read clearly and don't overlap.

The `keep` flag preserves existing positions where it can, so a re-run doesn't make the camera jump. It is the geometry step between *deciding* the topology and *drawing* it, and it re-runs whenever membership changes — including during a promotion, when a newly chosen sun needs its planets laid around it.

galaxy_pos_now.name: galaxyPosNow()
galaxy_pos_now.desc:
`galaxyPosNow(i)` returns a node's *current* on-screen galaxy position: its base coordinate with the galaxy's slow spin (the wheel angle) applied. Because the whole galaxy is always rotating, the stored base position isn't where a node actually is at this instant.

This is the small but essential correction that keeps everything aligned with what the viewer sees: picking, connector routing, label placement and the promotion swap all ask this function where a node *really* is right now, rather than trusting the un-rotated coordinates.

promote.name: promote()
promote.desc:
`promote(F, inPlace)` is the swap at the heart of focusing on a node. The chosen node F is turned into a sun — taking over a sun's slot in the galaxy — and its current neighbours are re-homed as its planets. In effect, whatever you point at becomes the centre of its own system, which is what makes *every* node explorable as a hub, not just the ones that began as suns.

With `inPlace` set, it performs the swap without a full re-layout, keeping the transition smooth rather than reshuffling the whole galaxy. It leans on `galaxyPosNow` to place things relative to what's currently on screen and on `buildSolarOrbits` to lay the new planets around the promoted node.

load_graph.name: loadGraph()
load_graph.desc:
`loadGraph(doc)` is the top-level act of putting a document on screen. It marks the graph clean, hands the document to `Model.load` to build the indexed model, refreshes the derived state — the highlights button, the visibility flags, the renderer's colours — and resets the view to show the new galaxy.

It sits above `Model.load`: where that builds the data model, `loadGraph` also updates all the UI and rendering that must follow a fresh document. It runs on first boot, when you open a different graph, and after a merge or example load.

synth_graph.name: synthGraph()
synth_graph.desc: `synthGraph(n)` generates a synthetic random graph of `n` nodes — assorted groups and random links — from a fixed seed. It is a testing and demo utility: a quick way to conjure a graph of arbitrary size to exercise layout, rendering and performance without a real dataset.

find_merge_match.name: findMergeMatch()
find_merge_match.desc: `findMergeMatch(nd2)` decides whether an incoming node already exists in the current graph, matching first on a shared URL and then on name. It is the identity check at the heart of merging: getting it right is what stops a merge from either duplicating nodes or wrongly fusing distinct ones.

fill_gaps.name: fillGaps()
fill_gaps.desc:
`fillGaps(dst, src, groupMap)` copies any fields `dst` is missing from `src` — description, url, image, group, subgraph and the like — without overwriting values `dst` already has. An optional `groupMap` translates the source's group id to the destination's, which is what lets a merge fold nodes in under matching groups.

This is now the single fill-gaps function: the earlier duplicate that silently shadowed it — disabling merge's group remapping — has been removed. Two-argument calls enrich as before; calls with a map also remap groups.

merge_into.name: mergeInto()
merge_into.desc:
`mergeInto(data2)` merges another document into the current graph rather than replacing it. It matches incoming nodes against existing ones through `findMergeMatch`, tops up matched nodes with any missing fields via the merge variant of `fillGaps` (remapping groups), adds the genuinely new nodes and links, and de-duplicates the result.

It is how two graphs are combined — folding a supplementary dataset into a main one, say — without losing either side's detail. Most of its length is that reconciliation: deciding what is the same, what is new, and how to translate groups between the two documents.

each_media_field.name: eachMediaField()
each_media_field.desc: `eachMediaField(ds, fn)` is a small recursive walker: for every node in a document, and every media field it can hold, it calls `fn(node, field)`, descending into any subgraphs. It is the shared traversal behind `hasBundleableMedia` (which checks for local media) and `stripLocalMedia` (which deletes it), so the node-by-field-by-subgraph walk lives in one place.

has_bundleable_media.name: hasBundleableMedia()
has_bundleable_media.desc: `hasBundleableMedia(ds)` reports whether a document contains any local, non-URL media worth bundling, scanning every node's media fields and recursing into subgraphs through the shared `eachMediaField` walker. `doExport` uses it to choose between a plain JSON export and a media-carrying zip.

collect_and_extract_media.name: collectAndExtractMedia()
collect_and_extract_media.desc: `collectAndExtractMedia(ds, zip, pathPrefix)` walks a document's nodes, and any subgraphs, moving each local media value — an embedded image or icon — out of the JSON and into a file inside the export zip, then rewriting the node to point at that path. It is what turns inline base64 media into properly bundled files, keeping the JSON small and the assets reusable.

rehydrate_images.name: rehydrateImages()
rehydrate_images.desc: `rehydrateImages(dataset, zip, pathPrefix)` is the import-side counterpart to bundling: when a document is loaded from a zip, it reads each bundled media file back out of the archive and restores it onto its node, so an imported bundle looks exactly like the graph that was exported.

parse_json_or_zip.name: parseJsonOrZip()
parse_json_or_zip.desc: `parseJsonOrZip(file)` reads an uploaded file into a document, handling both plain `.json` and `.zip` bundles. For a zip it unpacks the JSON and rehydrates the bundled media (which needs the JSZip library); for JSON it parses directly. It is the single entry point for turning any uploaded file into a loadable graph.

strip_local_media.name: stripLocalMedia()
strip_local_media.desc: `stripLocalMedia(ds)` removes every local, non-URL media value from a document, walking node media fields and subgraphs via the shared `eachMediaField`, to produce a lean media-free copy for a media-stripped export.
strip_local_media.code: function stripLocalMedia(ds){ eachMediaField(ds, (nd,f)=>{ if(nd[f] && !/^https?:/i.test(nd[f])) delete nd[f]; }); return ds; }

embed_media_base64.name: embedMediaBase64()
embed_media_base64.desc: `embedMediaBase64(ds)` is the inverse of bundling: it walks a document and inlines each referenced local media file as a base64 data URI directly on the node. It is used where a graph must be fully self-contained in a single JSON, every image carried inside it, rather than split across a bundle.
embed_media_base64.code: function embedMediaBase64(ds, seen){ seen=seen||new Set(); if(!ds||seen.has(ds)) return ds; seen.add(ds); for(const id of Object.keys(ds.nodes||{})){ const nd=ds.nodes[id]; for(const [f] of MEDIA_FIELDS){ const v=nd[f]; if(!v) continue; if(/^data:/i.test(v)||/^https?:/i.test(v)) continue; try{ const blob=await (await fetch(v)).blob(); nd[f]=await new Promise((res,rej)=>{ const r=new FileReader(); r.onload=()=>res(r.result); r.onerror=rej; r.readAsDataURL(blob); }); }catch(e){ delete nd[f]; } } if(nd.subgraph) await embedMediaBase64(nd.subgraph, seen); } for(const l of (ds.links||[])){ if(l&&l.subgraph) await embedMediaBase64(l.subgraph, seen); } for(const _r in (ds._subgraphs||{})) await embedMediaBase64(ds._subgraphs[_r], seen); return ds; }

do_export.name: doExport()
do_export.desc:
`doExport(dataset)` exports the current graph as a downloadable file. If the graph carries no bundleable media it writes a plain JSON document; if it has local images or icons, it offers to bundle them into a zip alongside the JSON so nothing is lost, and shows progress while it does. It builds a safe filename from the graph's title and hands over the download.

It is the outward half of portability — producing exactly the document shape the app reads back in. Most of its body is the choice between a lean JSON export and a media-bundled zip.

start_rename.name: startRename()
start_rename.desc: `startRename()` turns the graph's title into an editable text field in place, so the document can be renamed by clicking its title. It swaps the title text for an input and commits the new name back to the model on blur or Enter — a small inline-edit affordance for the one piece of top-level metadata.

reset_new_btn.name: resetNewBtn()
reset_new_btn.desc: `resetNewBtn()` disarms the New-graph button, cancelling its confirm timer and restoring its label. The New button is a two-tap confirm, so a graph is never wiped by a single accidental tap; this resets it when the confirm window lapses or is cancelled.
reset_new_btn.code:
function resetNewBtn(){ newArmed=false; if(newArmTimer){ clearTimeout(newArmTimer); newArmTimer=null; }
